title: Centre of mass
examples: How do I calculate the centre of mass for an irregularly shaped object?
Does the centre of mass always fall on the object?
What happens to the centre of mass when an object moves?

explain.say: Today we are learning about the centre of mass.
The centre of mass is a single point representing the average location of all the mass.
For two point masses, you find the COM using a weighted average formula.
When an object moves, its centre of mass moves according to the net external force.
If the net external force is zero, the centre of mass remains stationary or moves at constant velocity.
Consider a uniform rod balanced on a pivot point. The COM is exactly at its geometric center.

faq.q: Does the centre of mass always fall inside the object?
faq.a: No, the centre of mass can fall outside the physical object itself. This happens if the mass distribution is uneven.
asks: Is it possible for COM to leave the object?

faq.q: If the COM is stationary, does that mean the object is not moving?
faq.a: No, the object can still be rotating or translating while its COM remains fixed. Think of a spinning top.
asks: Can it spin but COM stays put?
Does COM stay put if it rotates?

faq.q: How do I calculate COM for a system of objects connected by ropes?
faq.a: You treat the entire system as a collection of point masses and use the weighted average formula for all masses together.
asks: Ropes connecting masses, how to find COM?

faq.q: Is the centre of mass the same as the centre of gravity?
faq.a: For objects near the Earth's surface, they are usually treated as the same. However, technically, the centre of gravity depends on the gravitational field.
asks: COM vs CG, what is the difference?
Are they interchangeable in physics problems?

faq.q: What if the forces acting are not purely horizontal or vertical?
faq.a: You must resolve all forces into horizontal and vertical components before applying Newton's second law to find the motion of the COM.

facts: The centre of mass is a weighted average of the positions of the object's mass.
If the net external force on a system is zero, the centre of mass has constant velocity.
The motion of the centre of mass is governed by Newton's second law: Fnet = M acom.
For two masses, m1 and m2, separated by distance d, the COM is located at (m1r1 + m2r2) / (m1 + m2).

quiz.say: Two masses, 2 kg and 3 kg, are placed on a line. The 2 kg mass is at position zero and the 3 kg mass is at position 6 meters. Where is the centre of mass?
quiz.why: The formula requires summing the product of each mass and its distance from the origin, then dividing by the total mass.

wrong.0: This only considers the ratio of the masses, ignoring the distance.
wrong.1: This assumes the COM is located at the position of the heavier mass.
wrong.2: This incorrectly averages the positions without weighting by mass.

quiz.say: A cart is pulled horizontally by a constant force, but friction is also acting. Which statement about the COM is true?

options.show: The COM accelerates only when the force is zero.
options.say: The COM accelerates only when the force is zero.

quiz.why: Since there is a net horizontal force, the centre of mass must accelerate in that direction.

wrong.0: Vertical forces are balanced, so acceleration is zero vertically.
wrong.1: Acceleration happens whenever there is a net force.
wrong.3: This ignores the net force causing acceleration.

quiz.say: If a system of masses is in equilibrium, what can be said about its centre of mass?

options.show: The centre of mass has zero acceleration.
options.say: The centre of mass has zero acceleration.

options.show: The system must be at rest.
options.say: The system must be at rest.

options.show: The centre of mass must be at the pivot point.
options.say: The centre of mass must be at the pivot point.

options.show: The centre of mass must be accelerating downwards.
options.say: The centre of mass must be accelerating downwards.

quiz.why: Zero net force means zero acceleration for the centre of mass.

wrong.1: It could be moving at a constant velocity.
wrong.2: Equilibrium only requires zero net force, not zero position.
wrong.3: Gravity is balanced by the normal force, resulting in zero net vertical force.
